Chloramphenicol markedly inhibits the metab- olism of tolbutamide and increases its half-life,1 which can result in hypoglycaemia. Sulfonamides,2 including co-trimoxazole,3-5 may also enhance the hypoglycaemic effects of the sulfonyl- ureas. There have been rare reports of elevated glibenclamide concentrations and hypoglycaemia when ciprofloxacin was giv- en to patients who were on stable glibenclamide therapy.6 For reports of hypoglycaemia when gatifloxacin was given to pa- tients already receiving a sulfonylurea (glimepiride in one case, and glibenclamide plus pioglitazone in another), see p.281. There have also been a few cases of severe hypoglycaemia when clarithromycin was added to glibenclamide or glipizide; renal impairment may have played a role in these cases.7 Rifampicin (and probably other rifamycins) can enhance the metabolism and decrease the effect of tolbutamide, chlorpropamide,8,9 and glibenclamide10 and dosage of the hypoglycaemic drug may need to be increased.
